topic: Jumper's knee: pain below the kneecap (patellar tendinopathy)

slides.headline: Jumper's knee: load it, don't lose it
slides.sub: Pain just below the kneecap when you jump, squat or take the stairs?

slides.title: Meet jumper's knee
slides.body: Patellar tendinopathy is irritation of the tendon just below the kneecap. It's common in basketball, volleyball and netball, and usually flares when jumping load climbs faster than the tendon can adapt.

slides.title: Rest calms it, load rebuilds it
slides.body: Stopping completely often settles the pain, but it tends to return once you're back on court. Tendons usually respond to gradual, planned loading, so adjust your training rather than stopping everything.

slides.title: Use a 0 to 10 pain scale
slides.body: Pain up to about 3 or 4 out of 10 during exercise is usually acceptable, as long as it settles by the next morning. If it's worse the next day, ease off a little.

slides.title: Holds first, jumps last
slides.body: Rehab often starts with holds, like a wall sit or leg press hold, then moves to slow squats, and later to jumping and landing. Progress over weeks to months is normal.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Sudden pain with a pop, quick swelling, the knee giving way, trouble straightening your leg, or pain that stops you walking normally are worth an assessment rather than waiting.

caption:
Pain just below the kneecap every time you jump, squat or take the stairs?

That's often patellar tendinopathy, also called jumper's knee. It usually shows up when jumping or squatting load increases faster than the tendon can adapt, like a new season, extra training or a switch to harder courts.

Rest tends to calm it down, but it often comes back once you return to sport. What usually helps more is adjusting your training and rebuilding tendon capacity gradually: holds, then slow strength work, then jumping and landing. Mild discomfort that settles by the next morning is usually OK.

A pop, rapid swelling, the knee giving way or trouble straightening it are worth getting checked sooner.

topic: Mat vs reformer Pilates: which one for you?

slides.headline: Mat or reformer: which suits you?
slides.sub: Both can build strength. The right one depends on you and your goals.

slides.title: Mat: your body is the load
slides.body: Mat Pilates uses bodyweight, gravity and small props like bands and balls. It's easy to keep going at home or while travelling, and it gets surprisingly hard once you slow the movements down.

slides.title: Reformer: springs change the load
slides.body: The reformer's springs can assist a movement or add resistance. That makes it easy to scale exercises up or down in small steps, which often suits people returning from injury or new to exercise.

slides.title: Who each one often suits
slides.body: Reformer can suit people who need support or adjustable load. Mat often suits people who want a routine they can take anywhere. Neither is better overall. It comes down to your needs.

slides.title: Many people use both
slides.body: A common mix is guided reformer sessions plus a short mat routine at home between visits. The home work often helps what you learn in the studio carry over into daily life.

slides.title: Clinical Pilates starts with a check
slides.body: In clinical Pilates, your first session looks at your history, goals and how you move. Your program is then set up on the mat, the reformer or both, and progressed as you get stronger.

topic: Meniscus tear: why surgery often isn't step one

slides.headline: Meniscus tear? Rehab usually comes first
slides.sub: For many knees, exercise-based rehab is the first step, not the operating theatre.

slides.title: What the meniscus does
slides.body: The menisci are two C-shaped cartilage pads that help spread load through the knee. Tears can happen with a twisting injury, and they also become more common with age, often without any pain.

slides.title: Why rehab usually comes first
slides.body: Current guidelines suggest that for many meniscus tears, especially ones that develop with age, exercise-based rehab is a sensible first step. Research suggests many people improve without an operation.

slides.title: What rehab often looks like
slides.body: Early on: settling swelling, getting the knee to straighten and bend, and walking comfortably. Then: gradual strength for the thighs and hips, plus balance, and later sport-specific drills.

slides.title: Clicking isn't always a problem
slides.body: Occasional clicking without pain or swelling is common in knees and often not a concern. What matters more is how your knee is working day to day, and whether it's improving over the weeks.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: A knee that locks and won't straighten, keeps giving way, swells quickly after an injury, or can't take your weight is worth a prompt assessment. Your GP or physio can guide the next step.

topic: Hip osteoarthritis: exercise comes first

slides.headline: Stiff, achy hip in the mornings?
slides.sub: Hip osteoarthritis is common, and exercise is usually the first thing to try.

slides.title: Hip OA is very common
slides.body: Osteoarthritis is a common change in the hip joint as we get older. It often shows up as a groin or front-of-hip ache, stiffness after sitting, and trouble putting on socks or shoes.

slides.title: Exercise is first-line care
slides.body: Current guidelines recommend exercise and education as first-line care for hip osteoarthritis, whatever the X-ray shows. Strength and movement can help with pain and daily function for many people.

slides.title: Four moves to start with
slides.body: Sit to stand from a chair, bridges, side-lying leg lifts and step-ups. Two or three sessions a week, building gradually over time, is a reasonable place to begin for most people.

slides.title: Keep walking, adjust the dose
slides.body: Walking, cycling and swimming are usually fine. Some ache during activity is OK if it settles within a day. If it doesn't, shorten the distance or slow the pace rather than stopping.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Hip pain after a fall, being unable to take weight, a hot swollen joint, fever, or pain that wakes you every night and keeps building should be checked by your GP promptly.

topic: Chiropractic care for lower back pain: what guidelines say

slides.headline: Back pain: what do guidelines recommend?
slides.sub: Where chiropractic care fits, and what matters just as much.

slides.title: Staying active comes first
slides.body: Current guidelines for lower back pain start with reassurance and staying active. Gentle walking and normal daily activity, adjusted to comfort, usually help more than bed rest.

slides.title: Manual therapy is an option
slides.body: Guidelines list spinal manipulation and mobilisation as options for some people, usually alongside exercise and advice. It can help with pain and movement in the short term, rather than as a stand-alone plan.

slides.title: Scans often aren't needed
slides.body: For most lower back pain without warning signs, guidelines don't recommend routine X-rays or MRI. Scans often show changes that are just as common in people who have no pain at all.

slides.title: Exercise carries the long game
slides.body: Strength and movement work, such as walking, Pilates-style exercise or a gym program, is recommended for back pain that lingers. The type matters less than finding one you'll keep doing.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Numbness around the groin, changes in bladder or bowel control, leg weakness, fever, unexplained weight loss, or pain after a significant fall need prompt medical attention.

topic: Shoulder pain lifting overhead at the gym

slides.headline: Shoulder pinches on overhead press?
slides.sub: A few training tweaks often let you keep lifting while it settles.

slides.title: Usually a load issue
slides.body: Shoulder pain with pressing overhead is common in gym-goers. It often follows a jump in weight, sets or training days, rather than one bad rep or a structural problem.

slides.title: Modify, don't necessarily stop
slides.body: Try a lighter weight, a slightly shorter range, or swap to a landmine press or incline press for a while. Keep the movements that feel OK so you can keep training.

slides.title: Train the upper back and cuff
slides.body: Rows, face pulls and side-lying or banded external rotations build the muscles that support overhead work. Two or three sessions a week is a reasonable start for most lifters.

slides.title: Rebuild overhead gradually
slides.body: Return to overhead pressing with lighter loads and more reps first. Use the next-day check: if the shoulder feels OK tomorrow, progress a little. If not, hold steady.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Sudden weakness after a fall or heavy lift, a shoulder that feels unstable or slips, night pain that keeps building, or tingling down the arm is worth an assessment.

topic: Golfer's elbow: pain on the inside of the elbow

slides.headline: Golfer's elbow isn't just for golfers
slides.sub: Inside-of-elbow pain is common in lifters, tradies and desk workers.

slides.title: What golfer's elbow is
slides.body: It's irritation of the tendons on the inside of the elbow that help bend the wrist and grip. It usually builds up gradually after a change in gripping, lifting or carrying.

slides.title: Common triggers
slides.body: A new gym program with heavy pulling, lots of tool use, carrying shopping or kids, a new sport, or long hours on a mouse can all add up. Usually it's the total load that matters.

slides.title: Ease the load, don't rest it all
slides.body: Try a lighter grip, lifting straps on heavy pulls, and splitting up repetitive tasks. Complete rest often calms it, but the tendon usually needs gradual loading to build capacity.

slides.title: A simple strength start
slides.body: Wrist curls with a light dumbbell, palm up, done slowly: 3 sets of 10 to 15 every second day. Mild discomfort that settles by the next day is usually OK.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Numbness or tingling into the ring and little fingers, sudden pain after a fall or heavy lift, swelling, or pain that keeps building despite easing off is worth getting checked.

topic: Tight calves in runners: where massage fits

slides.headline: Calves like concrete after runs?
slides.sub: Where remedial massage fits, and what does the heavy lifting.

slides.title: Why runners' calves tighten
slides.body: Your calves absorb a big share of the load on every stride. Mileage jumps, hills, speed work or new shoes can leave them feeling tight, heavy or cranky for a day or two.

slides.title: Where massage can help
slides.body: Remedial massage can help calves feel looser and less sore for a while, and many runners find it helps them feel ready for the next session. It's a helpful add-on, not the main treatment.

slides.title: Strength does the heavy lifting
slides.body: Calves that are strong enough for your training tend to feel less tight. Try slow single-leg calf raises, knee straight and bent, 3 sets to fatigue, two or three times a week.

slides.title: Timing your massage
slides.body: Leave a day or two between a firm remedial massage and a hard session or race. Lighter work closer to key runs usually suits better. Tell your therapist what's coming up.

slides.title: When it's more than tight
slides.body: Sudden sharp pain mid-run, a feeling of being kicked in the calf, bruising, swelling, or calf pain with redness and warmth should be checked by a physio or GP promptly.

topic: Carpal tunnel: tingling hands at night

slides.headline: Hands tingling in the middle of the night?
slides.sub: Carpal tunnel symptoms are common, and simple changes often help.

slides.title: What carpal tunnel involves
slides.body: The median nerve passes through a narrow tunnel at the wrist. When it's irritated, you may notice pins and needles in the thumb, index and middle fingers, often worse at night.

slides.title: Why nights are often worse
slides.body: Many people sleep with their wrists curled and bent, which can increase pressure in the tunnel. Shaking the hand out usually eases it for a while, which is something lots of people describe.

slides.title: Keep the wrist straight at night
slides.body: A wrist splint that keeps the wrist straight overnight is a common first step and can help night symptoms. Keeping your arms off and away from the pillow may help too.

slides.title: Adjust your daytime load
slides.body: Take short breaks from sustained gripping, tool use and phone scrolling. Keep your wrist level on the keyboard and mouse. Gentle nerve and tendon gliding exercises may also help.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Constant numbness, weakness in the thumb, dropping things, wasting at the base of the thumb, or symptoms with neck pain are worth an assessment soon rather than waiting it out.

slides.headline: Tired of tingling hands?
slides.body: Our Chatswood physios assess your wrist, neck and daily habits, then build a plan to help settle symptoms. Book online — link in bio.

Waking up at 3am shaking the pins and needles out of your hand?

topic: Wrist pain from push-ups and planks

slides.headline: Wrists grumble in push-ups and planks?
slides.sub: A few set-up changes and some strength work usually help.

slides.title: Why wrists complain
slides.body: Push-ups and planks put your wrist into full extension while it carries a lot of your bodyweight. If that's new, or your volume jumped quickly, the wrist often just needs time to adapt.

slides.title: Change the set-up first
slides.body: Spread your fingers, press through the knuckles and base of the fingers, and turn your hands slightly outward. Hands on a bench or wall reduce the load while it settles.

slides.title: Try a neutral wrist option
slides.body: Push-up handles, dumbbells or making a fist on a mat keep the wrist straighter. Forearm planks take the wrist out of it altogether and still train your trunk.

slides.title: Build wrist capacity
slides.body: Slow wrist curls and reverse curls, gentle rocking forward on hands and knees, and grip work two or three times a week help wrists handle more load over time.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain after a fall on an outstretched hand, swelling, painful clicking, a new lump, or pain on the thumb side that stays tender to press is worth an assessment.

slides.headline: Keep push-ups in your program
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD physios look at your wrist and your training, then plan a gradual path back to full push-ups and planks. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Push-ups and planks leaving your wrists sore?

Both put the wrist into full extension while it carries a lot of your bodyweight. If you've just started, or ramped up quickly, the wrist often just needs time and a bit of strength to catch up.

Start with the set-up: spread your fingers and press through the knuckles. Elevate your hands on a bench, use push-up handles or dumbbells, or switch to forearm planks for a while. Add slow wrist curls and gentle rocking on hands and knees a few times a week.

Pain after a fall on an outstretched hand, swelling or a new lump is worth getting checked.

topic: Bone stress injuries in runners

slides.headline: Bone pain that builds as you run
slides.sub: Bone stress injuries in runners: what they are and how to respond.

slides.title: Bone adapts, just slowly
slides.body: Bone gets stronger with running, but it adapts more slowly than muscle. When training jumps faster than bone can keep up, a bone stress injury can develop, ranging from a reaction to a fracture.

slides.title: Common signs to notice
slides.body: Pain that builds during a run instead of warming up, one spot on the bone that's tender to press, pain when hopping, or an ache that lingers after running are common signs.

slides.title: Common contributors
slides.body: Sudden jumps in mileage or speed work, harder surfaces, too little recovery, and not eating enough to match your training can all contribute. Often it's several things at once.

slides.title: This one needs a real break
slides.body: Unlike some niggles, bone stress usually needs a genuine reduction in running. Cycling or swimming can often continue, and a gradual return is planned once things settle.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Pain in one spot on the bone, pain with hopping, or pain at night or at rest is worth assessing. Your physio or GP may arrange imaging if a bone stress injury is suspected.

topic: Ankle still stiff months after a sprain

slides.headline: Ankle still stiff months after a sprain?
slides.sub: Common, and usually very trainable. Here's where to start.

slides.title: Why it lingers
slides.body: After a sprain, swelling, limping and moving less can leave the ankle stiff and weaker for months. Many people stop their rehab once the pain eases, before full movement comes back.

slides.title: Try the knee to wall test
slides.body: Face a wall with your foot about 10cm back. Bend your knee to touch the wall, heel down. Compare both sides. A big difference suggests there's movement worth getting back.

slides.title: Get the ankle bending again
slides.body: Do knee to wall rocks, 10 to 15 slow reps a few times a day, and add a band or weight as it improves. Calf stretches over the edge of a step can help too.

slides.title: Strength and balance matter
slides.body: Calf raises, single-leg balance and small hops rebuild the control that often drops off after a sprain. Research suggests balance training can help reduce the chance of another sprain.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: An ankle that keeps giving way, ongoing swelling, locking or catching, or pain in one spot that isn't improving is worth an assessment to look beyond a simple sprain.

slides.headline: Ankle not quite right?
slides.body: Our Chatswood physios assess movement, strength and balance, then build a plan to get your ankle moving and feeling confident. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Sprained your ankle months ago and it still feels stiff?

That's really common. Swelling, limping and moving less can leave an ankle stiff and weaker long after the pain settles, especially if rehab stopped early.

Try the knee to wall test: foot about 10cm from the wall, bend your knee to touch it with your heel down, and compare sides. If one side is much tighter, slow knee to wall rocks a few times a day are a good start. Add calf raises, single-leg balance and small hops to rebuild control.

An ankle that keeps giving way or stays swollen is worth an assessment.

topic: Pilates for neck and shoulder tension

slides.headline: Carrying your stress in your shoulders?
slides.sub: How clinical Pilates can help neck and shoulder tension feel easier.

slides.title: Tight often means overworked
slides.body: Neck and shoulder muscles often feel tight when they've been working hard for a long time: long desk days, stress, shallow breathing. Stretching feels good, but the relief can be short-lived.

slides.title: Breathe lower, shoulders drop
slides.body: Many people breathe mostly into the upper chest when busy or stressed. Pilates practises slower breathing into the lower ribs, which can help the neck and shoulder muscles ease off.

slides.title: Strengthen the upper back
slides.body: Reformer and mat exercises like rows, spring-loaded arm work and upper-back extension build the muscles that share the load with your neck, so it isn't doing all the work.

slides.title: Get your mid-back moving
slides.body: A stiff mid-back often leaves the neck doing more of the turning. Gentle rotation and extension work in Pilates helps spread movement through the whole spine.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Neck pain with pins and needles or weakness in the arm, headaches that keep building, dizziness, or pain after a fall or accident should be assessed before starting a program.

topic: Osteoporosis: strength training is safe and helpful

slides.headline: Osteoporosis? You can still lift weights
slides.sub: Guidelines now support strength and impact training for most people with low bone density.

slides.title: Bones respond to load
slides.body: Bone is living tissue that adapts to the forces placed on it. Current guidelines support progressive strength and impact exercise for most people with osteoporosis or low bone density.

slides.title: Why walking alone falls short
slides.body: Walking is great for general health, but on its own it often isn't enough load to strengthen bone. Research suggests supervised, progressive resistance training is generally safe and can help.

slides.title: What a program often includes
slides.body: Strength work like squats, deadlift variations and step-ups, building to moderate or heavier loads. Impact work such as heel drops or small jumps. And balance training to help reduce falls.

slides.title: Start guided, build gradually
slides.body: A physio can check your history, teach technique and start at a load that suits you, then progress it over weeks. Two or three sessions a week is a common target.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Sudden back pain after a minor bump or lift, noticeable loss of height, a fall with pain, or hip or groin pain when walking should be assessed by your GP or physio.

slides.headline: Want to train with confidence?

caption:
Diagnosed with osteoporosis and told to take it easy?

topic: Pain is not the same as damage

slides.headline: Hurt doesn't always mean harm
slides.sub: Why pain is a protective alarm, not a damage report.

slides.title: Pain is a protector
slides.body: Pain is your nervous system's way of protecting you. It's produced by the brain using many inputs, not just the state of your tissues. It's always real, but it isn't a direct measure of injury.

slides.title: Why the alarm gets sensitive
slides.body: When pain hangs around, the system can become more sensitive, like a smoke alarm that goes off when you make toast. Stress, poor sleep and worry can all turn the volume up.

slides.title: Scans don't tell the whole story
slides.body: Plenty of people without pain have disc bulges or joint changes on scans, and some people with a lot of pain have clear scans. The picture and the pain often don't match.

slides.title: Moving is usually safe
slides.body: For most persistent pain, some discomfort during exercise is OK and doesn't mean you're doing harm. Start small, build up gradually and check how you feel the next day.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: New pain after a significant injury, numbness or weakness, pain with fever or unexplained weight loss, or pain that's steadily getting worse is worth a proper assessment.

slides.headline: Want to understand your pain?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD physios take time to explain what's going on and build a plan to help you move with more confidence. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
If it hurts, does that mean something's damaged? Not always.

Pain is your nervous system's protection alarm. It's always real, but it's shaped by many things, including sleep, stress and past experiences, not just what's happening in your tissues. When pain lingers, the alarm can get more sensitive, like a smoke detector that goes off for toast.

That's why scan findings and pain levels often don't match, and why gradual movement is usually safe even when it's a bit uncomfortable.

New pain after an injury, numbness, weakness or pain that keeps getting worse is worth an assessment.

topic: Massage, stress and sleep

slides.headline: Stressed, wired and sleeping badly?
slides.sub: What remedial massage can and can't do for stress and sleep.

slides.title: Stress shows up in your body
slides.body: When you're stressed, muscles often tense, breathing gets quicker and shoulders creep up. Over weeks this can leave you feeling tight and achy, which makes switching off even harder.

slides.title: Where massage can help
slides.body: Many people feel calmer and more relaxed after a massage, and some sleep better that night. Research suggests massage can help people feel less tense in the short term.

slides.title: What it can't do alone
slides.body: Massage is a helpful add-on, not a treatment for ongoing sleep problems or high stress. If poor sleep or low mood keeps hanging around, it's worth talking to your GP.

slides.title: Keep the calm going
slides.body: Try a slow walk after your session, a warm shower before bed, and a few minutes of slow breathing with longer out-breaths. Regular movement during the day helps sleep too.

slides.title: Tell your therapist
slides.body: Let your therapist know if you'd like a calmer session with steady pressure, or if you want specific areas worked. Mention any health conditions or pregnancy before you start.

slides.headline: Need a proper reset?

topic: Woke up with a stiff neck (wry neck)

slides.headline: Woke up and can't turn your head?
slides.sub: Wry neck is common and usually settles within days to a week or so.

slides.title: What wry neck usually is
slides.body: Acute wry neck is sudden neck pain and stiffness, often noticed on waking, with the head held slightly to one side. It's common, and it usually settles well without anything serious going on.

slides.title: Keep it gently moving
slides.body: Small, comfortable movements every hour or so, turning, tilting and nodding within easy range, usually help more than holding it still. Aim for movement, not stretching into pain.

slides.title: Warmth and comfort help
slides.body: A heat pack for 15 to 20 minutes can help muscles ease off. Use a pillow that keeps your neck level, and carry on with normal activity as comfort allows.

slides.title: Where chiropractic care fits
slides.body: A chiropractor can assess your neck and may use gentle mobilisation, soft tissue work or an adjustment where appropriate, alongside simple exercises to keep things moving between visits.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Neck pain after a fall or accident, fever, a severe headache, pins and needles or weakness in the arm, dizziness, or trouble swallowing need prompt medical attention first.

slides.headline: Neck stuck on one side?
slides.body: Our chiropractors assess your neck, explain what's going on and give you simple ways to keep it moving. Book online — link in bio.

topic: Pacing for persistent pain: avoiding boom and bust

slides.headline: Big day, then three days on the couch?
slides.sub: That's boom and bust. Pacing can help you break the cycle.

slides.title: What boom and bust looks like
slides.body: On a good day you do everything: the garden, the gym, the lot. Pain flares, so you rest for days and lose fitness. Then the next good day starts the whole cycle again.

slides.title: Step 1: find your baseline
slides.body: Pick an activity, like walking. Work out how much you can do on a good day and on a bad day without a big flare. Start at a little less than the bad-day amount.

slides.title: Step 2: follow the plan, not pain
slides.body: Stick to your planned amount on good days too. Stop when you reach it, even if you feel fine. Break bigger jobs into chunks, with short rests in between.

slides.title: Step 3: build up slowly
slides.body: Every week or two, increase by a small amount. Around 10% is a common guide. Expect some ups and downs. A mild flare means hold steady, not start again from scratch.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: New or different pain, numbness or weakness, pain with fever or unexplained weight loss, or flares that keep getting worse despite pacing are worth an assessment.

slides.headline: Want a pacing plan?
slides.body: Our Chatswood physios help you set a baseline, plan your week and build activity back up gradually. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Great day, big effort, then three days paying for it?

That pattern is called boom and bust, and it's really common with persistent pain. The good days push too far, the flare forces rest, fitness drops and the cycle starts again.

Pacing breaks it. Find a baseline you can manage on a bad day, start just under it, and stick to the plan on good days too. Split bigger jobs into chunks. Then build up by small amounts every week or two. A mild flare means hold steady, not start over.

New pain, numbness or weakness is worth getting checked.

topic: Pilates during pregnancy

slides.headline: Can you do Pilates while pregnant?
slides.sub: For most people, yes, with some sensible changes as the weeks go on.

slides.title: Get the OK first
slides.body: Check with your GP, obstetrician or midwife before starting, especially if you have any pregnancy complications. Let our Pilates team know how many weeks along you are at every session.

slides.title: What it can help with
slides.body: Pilates can help you stay active, keep strength through the hips, back and legs, and practise breathing and pelvic floor work. Guidelines encourage regular moderate activity in most healthy pregnancies.

slides.title: Changes as you progress
slides.body: Later in pregnancy, lying flat on your back for long periods can make some people lightheaded, so positions shift to side-lying, sitting or inclined. Deep twists and heavy loads are usually modified.

slides.title: Pelvic floor: squeeze and let go
slides.body: Pelvic floor work isn't just squeezing. Learning to relax it matters too, especially heading towards birth. Breathing and gentle exercises in sessions can help with both.

slides.title: When to stop and get checked
slides.body: Stop and contact your care team if you have bleeding, fluid loss, dizziness, chest pain, calf pain or swelling, regular painful contractions, or reduced baby movements.

slides.headline: Staying strong through pregnancy
slides.body: Our Pilates team tailors sessions to your stage and history, alongside advice from your care team. Cover varies, so check with your fund. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Pregnant and wondering if Pilates is still OK?

For most healthy pregnancies, yes. Guidelines encourage regular moderate activity, and Pilates can help you keep strength through the hips, back and legs while practising breathing and pelvic floor work, including learning to relax it, not just squeeze.

Get the OK from your GP, obstetrician or midwife first. As the weeks go on, sessions usually move away from lying flat on your back and ease off deep twists and heavy loads.

Stop and contact your care team if you notice bleeding, fluid loss, dizziness or reduced baby movements.
